title: Is My Phone Listening to Me?
objective: After this level you can weigh the evidence on whether phones secretly record conversations for ads, and the simpler explanations for eerie ads.
summary: A 2018 test of 17,000+ Android apps found none secretly sending audio, but found apps sending screen recordings. Location, browsing and app data explain eerie ads.

cards.headline: You mention hiking boots. An hour later, a boot ad.
cards.body: It feels like proof that your phone is listening. Some researchers decided to test it instead of guessing. What they found is less spooky than the rumor, and in one way more surprising.

cards.headline: The test: 17,000 apps
cards.body: In a 2018 study, Northeastern University researchers ran more than 17,000 popular Android apps with an automated test program and watched what each one sent out. They were looking for the microphone switching on and audio leaving the phone. They found no app doing it. That's strong evidence, not proof: it covered the Android apps they could test, not every app on every phone.

cards.headline: What they found instead
cards.body: The surprise was the screen. Some apps sent screenshots and screen recordings to other companies without telling the user. One food-delivery app sent its screens to an analytics firm. So the leak the study actually found wasn't your voice. It was whatever happened to be on your screen.

cards.headline: The boring explanation
cards.body: Ads don't need your voice. Your phone's GPS and nearby cell towers reveal where you go, tracking pixels on websites record what you browse and put in your cart, and companies combine data from many apps into one profile. That's usually enough to guess at hiking boots. And you can check the microphone yourself: on an iPhone with iOS 14 or later, an orange dot appears when an app is using it, and a green dot when the camera is on too.

cards.headline: Listening: checked
learned: A 2018 test of 17,000+ apps found no secret audio sending
It did find apps sending screen recordings
Location, browsing and app profiles explain eerie ads
On an iPhone, an orange dot shows the microphone is in use

questions.prompt: What did the 2018 Northeastern study of more than 17,000 Android apps find about microphones?

options.label: Most of the apps recorded audio and sent it off for ads
options.rationale: The study found no app doing this.

options.label: No app was caught secretly switching on the microphone to send audio
Only free apps switched on the microphone to listen
options.rationale: No app was found sending audio.

options.label: Apps listened in secret, but only while phones charged
options.rationale: No secret listening was found at all.

questions.explanation: The team found no app secretly activating the microphone and sending audio, though it tested only the apps it could.

questions.prompt: You talk about a camping trip, then see a tent ad. Which explanation fits the evidence best?

options.label: The phone recorded you and sent the audio to advertisers
options.rationale: The large app study found no secret audio leaks.

options.label: Ads are chosen at random, so it's pure luck
options.rationale: Ads are targeted using data about you.

options.label: Location, browsing and app data had already pointed to camping
The ad company read your text messages
options.rationale: Nothing in the evidence shows that; tracking data is enough.

questions.explanation: Location, browsing and combined app profiles explain targeted ads without any microphone, and the big study found no secret listening.

questions.prompt: The researchers watched for audio leaving phones. From Level 5, what would recorded sound be inside a phone?

options.label: A grid of pixels, each with red, green and blue values
One single number standing for the whole recording
options.rationale: Sound needs thousands of measurements a second.

options.label: A list of letters written down in the ASCII code
Samples: measurements of the sound wave stored as binary numbers

questions.explanation: Digital sound is a stream of samples, each a measurement of the wave written as a binary number.
